ho.e: From Middle English ho, hoo (interjection), from Old English hō, probably from Old Norse hó! (interjection, also, a shepherd's call).
ho.g: Used to attract attention to something sighted, usually by lookouts.

ho.e: From Middle English howe, houwe, hoȝe, from Old English hogu and hoga, from Proto-Germanic *hugô, *hugiz, *huguz (“mind, thought, understanding”), akin to Old High German hugu, hugi (Middle High German hüge), Old Saxon hugi (Middle Dutch höghe, Dutch heug), Old Norse hugr, Gothic 𐌷𐌿𐌲𐍃 (hugs).

hoar.e: From Middle English hor, hore, from Old English hār (“hoar, hoary, grey, old”), from Proto-West Germanic *hair, from Proto-Germanic *hairaz (“grey”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ḱeh₃- (“grey, dark”).

hoard.e: From Middle English hord, from Old English hord (“an accumulation of valuable objects cached for preservation or future use; treasure; hoard”), from Proto-West Germanic *hoʀd, from Proto-Germanic *huzdą (“treasure; hoard”), of unknown origin, but possibly derived from Proto-Indo-European *kewdʰ- (“to conceal, hide”), thus meaning “something hidden”.
From Middle English horden, from Old English hordian, from Proto-West Germanic *hoʀdōn.
hoard.g: To amass, usually for one's own private collection.

hoarder.e: From Middle English horder, hordere (“a keeper of a store of goods”), from Old English hordere (“a treasurer, steward, chamberlain”), equivalent to hoard + -er.
hoarder.g: One who hoards; one who accumulates, collects, and stores, especially one who does so to excess.

hoary.e: Possibly from Middle English *hori (suggested by horilocket (“hoary-locked, having hoary locks or curls”)), equivalent to hoar + -y. Alternatively, Middle English horilocket may represent Middle English hor (“hoar, hoary”) + ilocket (“locked”) rather than hori (“hoary”) + locket (“locked”).

hoe.e: From Middle English howe, from Anglo-Norman houe, from Frankish *hauwā, derivative of Frankish *hauwan (“to hew”), from Proto-Germanic *hawwaną.
hoe.g: Any of various tools for scraping, scratching, digging, or stirring soil or other materials.

hoe.e: From a non-rhotic pronunciation of whore.

hoise.e: Probably from Middle Dutch hisen (modern Dutch hijsen) or Middle Low German hissen.

hoist.e: Alteration of earlier hoise (“to hoist”), apparently based on the past tense forms, from Middle Dutch hisen (“to hoist”).
hoist.g: To raise; to lift; to elevate (especially, to raise or lift to a desired elevation, by means of tackle or pulley, said of a sail, a flag, a

hold.e: From Middle English holden, derived from Old English healdan, derived from Proto-West Germanic *haldan, derived from Proto-Germanic *haldaną (“to tend, herd”), maybe derived from Proto-Indo-European *kel- (“to drive”).

From Middle English hold, holde, from Old English hold (“gracious, friendly, kind”), from Proto-West Germanic *holþ, from Proto-Germanic *hulþaz (“favourable, gracious, loyal”), from Proto-Indo-European *kel- (“to tend, incline, bend, tip”).

holding.e: From hold + -ing. The sense "holding company" is from Russian холдинг (xolding), itself a pseudo-anglicism derived from an ellipsis of holding company.
holding.g: Something that one owns, especially stocks and bonds.

hole.e: From Middle English hole, hol, from Old English hol (“orifice, hollow place, cavity”), from Proto-West Germanic *hol (“hole”), from Proto-Germanic *hulą (“hollow space, cavity”), noun derivative of Proto-Germanic *hulaz (“hollow”), which is of uncertain ultimate origin.
hole.g: A hollow place or cavity; an excavation; a pit; a dent; a depression; a fissure.

holiday.e: From Middle English halyday, holyday, halidei, haliȝdei, from Old English hāliġdæġ (“holy day, Sabbath”), equivalent to holy + day.
holiday.g: A day on which a religious event or secular celebration is traditionally observed.

holily.e: From Middle English holily, holyly, holilie, holiliche, holyliche, haliliche, haliʒlike, haliliʒ, from Old English hāliġlīċe, equivalent to holy + -ly.
holily.g: In a holy way; with sanctity.

holiness.e: From Middle English holynesse, holinesse, halinesse, from Old English hāliġnes (“holiness, a holy thing, rites”), from Proto-West Germanic *hailagnassī, equivalent to holy + -ness.
holiness.g: The state or condition of being holy.

hollow.e: From Middle English holow, holowe, holwe, holwȝ, holgh, from Old English holh (“a hollow”), from Proto-West Germanic *holh, from Proto-Germanic *hulwiją, from Proto-Germanic *hulaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to cover, hide”).
From Middle English holowe, holwe, holuȝ, holgh, from the noun (see above).
hollow.g: Having an empty space or cavity inside.

holy.e: From Middle English ali, aly, hale, halege, hali, halȝe, hayly, holi, holia, holie, holiȝ, holy, hooly, oli, oly, wholy, woly, from Old English hāleġ, hāliġ (“holy, sacred; healthy, sound”), from Proto-West Germanic *hailag, from Proto-Germanic *hailagaz (“holy, sacred”), from Proto-Germanic *hailaz (“healthy; whole”).
holy.g: Dedicated to a religious purpose or a god.

homage.e: From Middle English homage, from Old French homage, hommage, from Medieval Latin homināticum (“homage, the service of a vassal or 'man'”), from Latin homō (“a man, in Medieval Latin a vassal”) + -āticum (noun-forming suffix).
homage.g: A demonstration of respect, as towards a person after his or her retirement or death.

home.e: From Middle English hom, from Old English hām, from Proto-West Germanic *haim, from Proto-Germanic *haimaz (“home, village”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱóymos (“village, home”), from the root *tḱey-.

homeland.g: The country that one regards as home.

homeless.e: From Middle English *homles, *hamles, from Old English hāmlēas (“homeless”), equivalent to home + -less.
homeless.g: Lacking a permanent place of residence.

homer.e: From Hebrew חומר / חֹמֶר (khómer, “clay, heap, large unit of volume”).
homer.g: A former Hebrew unit of dry volume, about equal to 230 L or 6+¹⁄₂ US bushels.

homestead.e: From Middle English hamstede, hemstede (attested in placenames), from Old English hāmstede (“homestead”), from Proto-West Germanic *haimastadi (“homestead”). By surface analysis, home + stead.
homestead.g: A house together with surrounding land and buildings, especially on a farm; the property comprising these.

homosexual.e: Borrowed from German homosexual, from homo- (“same”) + sexual (“relating to sex or sexuality”), coined by Karl Maria Kertbeny in 1868, and popularized in Richard von Krafft-Ebing's Psychopathia Sexualis (2nd ed. 1887, in German) and Charles Gilbert Chaddock's 1892 English translation thereof (compare bisexual), displacing the slightly older term Uranian.
homosexual.g: Sexually and/or romantically attracted to members of the same sex, such as a man who is attracted to other men or a woman who is attracted t

honest.e: From Middle English honest, honeste (“honourable, appropriate, excellent”), from Old French honeste, from Latin honestus, from honor. For the verb, see Latin honestāre (“to clothe or adorn with honour”), and compare French honester.
honest.g: Scrupulous with regard to telling the truth; not given to swindling, lying, or fraud; upright.

honestly.e: From Middle English honestly, honestlyche, honestliche, equivalent to honest + -ly.

honesty.e: From Middle English honeste (“honour, integrity”), from Old French honesté (compare modern French honnêteté). By surface analysis, honest + -y. The plant is named so after the visibility of the seeds through the translucent pods.
honesty.g: The act, quality, or condition of being honest.

honey.e: From Middle English hony, honi, from Old English huniġ, from Proto-West Germanic *hunag, from Proto-Germanic *hunagą (compare Saterland Frisian Hunich, West Frisian hunich, German Low German Honnig, German Honig).
honey.g: A sweet, viscous, gold-colored fluid produced from plant nectar by bees, and often consumed by humans.

honeycomb.e: The English word is analysable as honey + comb. The Oxford English Dictionary posits that the arrangement of several plates of wax “hanging parallel to each other from the roof of the hive suggests a comb with its teeth”.
honeycomb.g: A substance made by bees (clade Anthophila) primarily from beeswax which has hexagonal cells to hold their larvae, and for storing pollen an

honor.e: From Middle English honour, honor, honur, from Anglo-Norman honour, honur, from Old French honor, from Latin honor.
honor.g: Recognition of importance or value; respect; veneration (of someone, usually for being morally upright or successful).

honorable.e: From Middle English honourable, from Old French honorable, honurable, from Latin honōrābilis, from honōrō (“to honour”); cognate with Italian onorabile, Spanish honorable. By surface analysis, honor + -able. In this sense, largely displaced Old English ārfæst.
honorable.g: Behaving in a manner that shows honor; decent, having integrity.

honourable.e: From Middle English honourable, from Old French honorable, honurable, from Latin honōrābilis, from honōrō (“to honour”); cognate with Italian onorabile, Spanish honorable. By surface analysis, honour + -able. In this sense, largely displaced Old English ārfæst.

honoureth.e: From honour + -eth, the archaic third-person singular present tense suffix.

hood.e: From Middle English hood, hod, from Old English hōd, from Proto-West Germanic *hōd, from Proto-Germanic *hōdaz, from Proto-Indo-European *kadʰ- (“to cover”).
hood.g: A covering for the head, usually attached to a larger garment such as a jacket or cloak.

hoof.e: From Middle English hof, houf, houve, hove, from Old English hōf, from Proto-Germanic *hōfaz (compare West Frisian hoef, Dutch hoef, German Huf, Danish hov, Norwegian hov, Swedish hov), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱoph₂ós (compare Sanskrit शफ (śaphá, “hoof, claw”), Avestan 𐬯𐬀𐬟𐬀 (safa, “hoof”), possibly Czech, Polish kopyto).
hoof.g: The tip of a toe of an ungulate such as a horse, ox or deer, strengthened by a thick keratin covering.

hook.e: From Middle English hoke, from Old English hōc (“angle, point, hook”), from Proto-West Germanic *hōk, from Proto-Germanic *hōkaz, variant of *hakô (“hook”), probably ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kog-, *keg-, *keng- (“peg, hook, claw”).
hook.g: A rod bent into a curved shape, typically with one end free and the other end secured to a rope or other attachment.

hoopoe.e: Alteration of obsolete hoopoop, from earlier hoop, from Middle French and Old French huppe, from Latin upupa, ultimately onomatopoeic;.
hoopoe.g: Any Old World bird of genus Upupa, especially Upupa epops (Eurasian hoopoe), known for its distinctive plumage, fanlike crest, and slender b

hope.e: From Middle English hopen, from Old English hopian (“hope”), from Proto-West Germanic *hopōn; further etymology unclear.
hope.g: To want (something) to happen, with a sense of expectation that it might [with that (+ clause); or (informal) with clause; or with so or (ne

hope.e: From Middle English hope, from Old English hopa (“hope, expectation”), from the same source as the verb hope. Eclipsed non-native early modern English esperance, borrowed from Middle French esperance.
hope.g: The feeling of trust, confidence, belief or expectation that something wished for can or will happen.

hopeless.g: Without hope; despairing; not expecting anything positive.

hopping.e: Alternative spelling (C17) of hoppe, from Middle French houbelon.
hopping.g: hop picking, the practice of picking hops; for Londoners a holiday period working in the hop gardens of Kent.

horde.e: From Middle French horde, from German Horde, from Polish horda, from Russian орда́ (ordá, “horde, clan, troop”), probably from Kipchak Turkic (compare Tatar урда (urda, “horde”)), ultimately from Proto-Turkic *ordu (“place of staying of the army, ruler etc.”).
horde.g: A wandering troop or gang; especially, a clan or tribe of a nomadic people (originally Tatars) migrating from place to place for the sake of

horizon.e: From Middle English orisonte, orisoun, from Middle French horizon, horizonte, from Old French orisonte, orison, via Latin horizōn, from Ancient Greek ὁρίζων (horízōn), from ὅρος (hóros, “boundary”).
horizon.g: The visible horizontal line (in all directions) where the sky appears to meet the earth in the distance.

horn.e: From Middle English horn, horne, from Old English horn, from Proto-West Germanic *horn, from Proto-Germanic *hurną. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱr̥h₂-nó-m, from *ḱerh₂- (“head, horn”).
horn.g: A hard growth of keratin that protrudes from the top of the head of certain animals, usually paired.

hornet.e: From Middle English hernet, from Old English hyrnetu, hyrnete, from Proto-West Germanic *hurnutu, from Proto-Germanic *hurznutō (compare German Hornisse), alteration of Proto-Germanic *hursulǭ (compare Dutch horzel), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱr̥h₂sro- (“hornet”, literally “the one with horns (antennae)”).
hornet.g: Any large wasp of the genus Vespa, having a brown-and-yellow-striped body and the ability to inflict a serious sting.

horrendous.e: Borrowed from Latin horrendus, future passive participle (gerundive) of horreō (“to dread”) + -ous.

horribly.e: From Middle English horribly, horribely, horribliche, horriblelyche, equivalent to horrible + -ly.
horribly.g: In a horrible way; very badly.

horrify.e: From horror + -ify, or borrowed from Latin horrificare (cf. French horrifier). 1791, in form horrifying.
horrify.g: To cause to feel extreme apprehension or unease; to cause to experience horror.

horror.e: From Middle English horer, horrour, from Old French horror, from Latin horror (“a bristling, a shaking, trembling as with cold or fear, terror”), from horrere (“to bristle, shake, be terrified”).
horror.g: An intense distressing emotion of fear or repugnance.

horse.e: From Middle English hors, horse, ors, from Old English hors (“horse”), from Proto-West Germanic *hors, *hross, from Proto-Germanic *hrussą (“horse”), most likely from Proto-Indo-European *ḱr̥sós (“vehicle”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers- (“to run”).
horse.g: A hoofed mammal, Equus ferus caballus, often used throughout history for riding and draft work.

horse.e: From Middle English horsen, from Old English horsian (“to horse, provide with horses”) and ġehorsian (“to horse, set or mount on a horse, supply with horses”), from the noun (see above).

horseback.e: From Middle English horsebacke, horsebak, horsbak, equivalent to horse + back.

horseman.e: From Middle English horsman, equivalent to horse + man.
horseman.g: A man who rides a horse.

hosen.e: From Middle English hosen, from Old English hosan (“hosen, leggings, trousers”), plural of hosa (“hose, legging, stocking”); reinforced by German Hosen (“trousers, pants”). Equivalent to hose + -en (plural ending).
hosen.g: Coverings for the legs; trousers; pants.

hospitable.e: Borrowed from Middle French hospitable, formed from the root of Latin hospitare with the suffix -able.

hospitality.e: From Middle English hospitalite, from Old French hospitalité (modern French hospitalité), from Latin hospitālitās (“hospitality”), from hospitālis (“hospitable”), from hospes (“guest", "host”).
hospitality.g: The act or service of welcoming, receiving, hosting, or entertaining guests; an appropriate attitude of openness, respect, and generosity to

host.e: From Middle English hoste, from Old French oste (French: hôte), from Latin hospitem, accusative of hospes (“a host, also a sojourner, visitor, guest; hence, a foreigner, a stranger”), from *hostipotis, an old compound of hostis and the root of potis, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰóstipotis (“master of guests”).
host.g: One which receives or entertains a guest, socially, commercially, or officially.

host.e: From Middle English oost, borrowed from Old French ost, oste, hoste, from Latin hostis (“foreign enemy”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰóstis (as opposed to inimicus (“personal enemy”)).
host.g: A multitude of people arrayed as an army; used also in religious senses, as: Heavenly host (of angels)

hostage.e: From Middle English hostage, ostage, from Old French hostage, ostage. This, in turn, is either from Old French hoste (“host”) + -age (in which case the sense development is from taking someone into "lodging" to taking them into "captivity", to applying the term to a captive), or is from Vulgar Latin obsidāticum (“condition of being held captive”).
hostage.g: A person given as a pledge or security for the performance of the conditions of a treaty or similar agreement, such as to ensure the status

hostile.e: Borrowed from Middle French hostile, from Latin hostīlis, from hostis (“enemy”).
hostile.g: Not friendly; appropriate to an enemy; showing the disposition of an enemy; showing ill will and malevolence or a desire to thwart and injur

hostility.e: From Middle English hostilitie, hostilite, from Old French hostilité, from Latin hostīlitās. By surface analysis, hostile + -ity.

hot.e: From Middle English hot, hoot, from Old English hāt (“hot”), from Proto-West Germanic *hait, from Proto-Germanic *haitaz (“hot”), from Proto-Indo-European *keHy- (“to heat; to become hot”). Superseded non-native Middle English chaud, from Old French chaut (“hot”); and early Modern English calent, from Latin calēns (“hot”).
hot.g: Relating to heat and conditions which produce it.

hotly.e: From Middle English *hotly, *hatliche, from Old English hātlīċe (“ardently, fervently”); equivalent to hot + -ly.

hough.e: From Middle English hough, houȝ, hoch, howghe, from Old English hōh (“heel, hough”), from Proto-West Germanic *hą̄h, from Proto-Germanic *hanhaz (“heel”). The regular modern English development would be /hʌf/, /haʊ/; this has been replaced by /hɒk/, originating in the compound huxen (also *hoxen), from Old English hōhsinu.
hough.g: Alternative form of hock (“the hollow behind the knee”).

hough.e: From Middle English ho, howe, hogh, from Old English hōh (“a promontory”).

hound.e: From Middle English hound, from Old English hund, from Proto-West Germanic *hund, from Proto-Germanic *hundaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱwṓ.
hound.g: A dog, particularly a breed with a good sense of smell developed for hunting other animals.

hound.e: From Middle English hounden, from the noun (see above).

hour.e: From Middle English houre, hour, oure, from Old French houre, from Latin hōra (“hour”), from Ancient Greek ὥρα (hṓra, “any time or period, whether of the year, month, or day”), from Proto-Indo-European *yóh₁r̥ (“year, season”). Partly displaced native Old English tīd (“time, hour”), whence Modern English tide.
hour.g: A unit of time of one twenty-fourth of a day (sixty minutes).

house.e: From Middle English hous, hus, from Old English hūs (“dwelling, shelter, house”), from Proto-West Germanic *hūs, from Proto-Germanic *hūsą (“house”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kews-, from *(s)kewH- (“to cover, hide”). Eclipsed non-native Middle English mees, meson, measoun (“house”), borrowed from Anglo-Norman mes, mies, meis, maisun (“house”).
house.g: A structure built or serving as an abode of human beings.

house.e: From Middle English housen, from Old English hūsian, from Proto-Germanic *hūsōną (“to house, live, dwell”), from the noun (see above).
house.g: To keep within a structure or container.

household.e: From Middle English houshold. By surface analysis, house + hold.
household.g: All the persons who live in a given house or other home; a family including attendants, servants etc.; a domestic or family establishment.

householder.e: From Middle English housholdere, equivalent to household + -er. The Buddhist sense is a semantic loan from Pali gahapati (literally “house-master”).

hover.e: Hoven is probably derived from Old English *hōfian, from hōfon, the plural past indicative form of hebban (“to lift, raise”), from Proto-West Germanic *habbjan, from Proto-Germanic *habjaną (“to lift; to heave”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *keh₂p- (“to hold, seize”).
hover.g: To keep (something, such as an aircraft) in a stationary state in the air.

how.e: From Middle English how, hou, hu, hwu, from Old English hū, from Proto-West Germanic *hwō, from Proto-Germanic *hwō (“through what, how”), from the same root as hwæt (“who, what”). /hw/ > /h/ due to wh-cluster reduction in Old English.
From Middle English howe, hough, hogh, partly from Old English hōh (“promontory”), and partly from Old Norse haugr (“a how, mound”).
how.g: An artificial barrow or tumulus; in later folklore, associated with fairies.

howbeit.e: Univerbation of how + be + it, literally “however it be”.

however.e: From Middle English however, how-ever, how-evere; equivalent to how + -ever.
however.g: Nevertheless; yet, still; in spite of that.

howl.e: From Middle English howlen, houlen, from Old English *hūlian, from Proto-West Germanic *hūilōn, from Proto-Germanic *hūwilōną, *hiuwilōną (“to howl”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *kū-, *kew- (“to howl, scream”). Likely of imitative origin.
howl.g: The protracted, mournful cry of a dog, wolf or other canid; also of other animals.

howling.e: From Middle English howlinge, howlynge, equivalent to howl + -ing (present participle ending).

howsoever.e: From Middle English howsoevere, how-so-evere, how so evere. By surface analysis, how + so + ever.
howsoever.g: Regardless of the way in which.

help.e: From Middle English help, from Old English help (“help, aid, assistance, relief”), from Proto-Germanic *helpō (“help”), *hilpiz, *hulpiz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱelb-, *ḱelp- (“to help”).
help.g: Action given to provide assistance; aid.

help.e: From Middle English helpen, from Old English helpan (“to help, aid, assist, benefit, relieve, cure”), from Proto-West Germanic *helpan, Proto-Germanic *helpaną (“to help”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱelb-, *ḱelp- (“to help”).
help.g: To provide assistance to (someone or something).
